nameStory: The name "brittle cinder" perfectly captures this fungus's appearance and texture. When mature, it develops a charcoal-black, crusty surface that looks remarkably like burned wood or cinders from a fire. Touch it and you'll understand the "brittle" part - the surface crumbles easily between your fingers, just like actual charcoal.
description: Brittle cinder is a wood-decaying fungus that forms hard, crusty growths on the trunks and roots of deciduous trees. It starts as small white or grayish patches but develops into large, black, coal-like crusts that can spread over several feet of bark surface. This fungus is actually a serious tree pathogen, causing root and butt rot that can eventually kill its host tree. The fruiting body feels remarkably similar to charcoal - hard, brittle, and crumbly to the touch.

idTips.label: Charcoal-like surface
idTips.description: The mature fungus looks exactly like chunks of charcoal stuck to tree bark - jet black, hard, and brittle with a rough, cracked texture that crumbles when rubbed

idTips.label: White early stage
idTips.description: Young growth appears as white to light gray crusty patches that gradually darken to black over time, often with white edges still visible

idTips.label: Tree location
idTips.description: Always found on deciduous trees, typically at the base of trunks or on exposed roots, occasionally extending up the lower trunk

idTips.label: Crusty texture
idTips.description: Surface feels like rough sandpaper or pumice stone, breaking off in small black fragments when scratched with a fingernail

idTips.label: Size and spread
idTips.description: Forms irregular patches that can cover large areas, sometimes wrapping partially around tree bases and spreading in connected clusters

habitat: Brittle cinder grows on deciduous trees throughout New England's forests, particularly favoring older hardwood stands with oak, maple, beech, and ash trees. Look for it in mature woodlands, parks, and suburban areas where large deciduous trees are present. It's most commonly found at the base of trees where roots meet the trunk, often in areas with rich, moist soil.

seasonality.spring: Existing crusts become more visible as snow melts, and you may spot fresh white patches beginning to develop on infected trees. The contrast against fresh spring bark makes identification easier.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season shows the most dramatic color transition from white to gray to black. Humid conditions help the fungus spread and develop its characteristic crusty texture.
seasonality.fall: Mature black crusts are at their most prominent and brittle. This is the best time to observe the full charcoal-like appearance and crumbly texture.
seasonality.winter: Snow cover may hide lower growths, but the black crusts remain visible on exposed trunk areas. The fungus stays dormant but retains its distinctive appearance.

funFact: This fungus is so good at mimicking charcoal that people have actually tried to use it as fuel - and it will burn! However, it's also known as the "death fungus" because infected trees often die within a few years, making it one of the most feared fungi among arborists and tree care professionals.
confusionNotes: The biggest confusion is with actual fire damage or charcoal residue on trees. Remember: real charcoal from fires usually appears in patches with obvious burn patterns, while brittle cinder grows in more organic, spreading shapes and often has white growing edges. If you're unsure, look for the characteristic white-to-black color progression at the margins.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name suggesting it's related to fire, brittle cinder has nothing to do with actual burning. The name can be misleading since people sometimes mistake it for fire damage on trees. It's also worth noting that this fungus is considered a serious forest pathogen, so finding it often indicates a tree is in decline.
compareHints: Brittle cinder is the only Kretzschmaria species commonly found in New England, but it can be confused with other black crusty fungi in the Xylariaceae family. However, most similar species don't develop the distinctive charcoal-like brittleness or show the same white-to-black color progression. The crumbly, coal-like texture when mature is virtually diagnostic for this species.
